questions.question: For f(x) = (x²−1)/(x−1), the function is undefined at x = 1 yet the limit exists. Explain what a limit measures that a value does not.
questions.solution: The limit describes the behaviour of f as x APPROACHES 1 from both sides — f(x) → 2 — regardless of what happens AT x = 1. A value needs the point to be defined; a limit only needs the neighbourhood to settle. Removing the hole (defining f(1) = 2) makes the function continuous, but the limit existed even without it.

questions.question: Why can't you 'simplify' 0/0 to 1 (since x/x = 1)? What does the symbol 0/0 actually signal?
questions.solution: 0/0 is not a number — it is a WARNING that both numerator and denominator vanish simultaneously, and the LIMIT depends on HOW fast each approaches zero. In (x²−1)/(x−1) the numerator vanishes faster, giving limit 2; in sin x / x it gives 1. Factor or transform to expose the real ratio — never treat 0/0 as arithmetic.

questions.question: A student applies L'Hôpital to lim(x→1) (x²−1)/(x−1) and gets 2. State the conditions that must hold before the rule may be used, and give a case where applying it blindly loops forever.
questions.solution: Conditions: the limit must be of the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, and the DERIVATIVE quotient's limit must exist. Blindly applying it to lim(x→∞) (x + sin x)/x differentiates forever (the oscillation never resolves) — the limit does not exist, so the rule never applies. Check the form first, then the existence of the resulting limit.

questions.question: f(x) = |x|/x. Find both one-sided limits at 0 and state whether f is continuous there.
questions.solution: x → 0⁺: |x|/x = x/x = 1. x → 0⁻: |x|/x = −x/x = −1. One-sided limits differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist and f is discontinuous at 0 (a jump discontinuity). Continuity requires the two sides to agree — the absolute-value trick is the standard test case.

questions.question: Evaluate lim(x→0) x²·sin(1/x) and explain why the squeeze theorem is needed rather than the product rule for limits.
questions.solution: −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1, so −x² ≤ x²·sin(1/x) ≤ x²; both bounds → 0, so the limit is 0. The product rule needs BOTH factors to have limits, but sin(1/x) has none (it oscillates). Squeezing between two functions with the same limit handles oscillation that no other tool reaches.

questions.question: State the three conditions for f to be continuous at a point a, and use them to check f(x) = (x+2)/(x−2) at x = 2.
questions.solution: (1) f(a) is defined; (2) lim(x→a) f(x) exists; (3) the limit equals f(a). At x = 2: f(2) is undefined (denominator zero) — condition 1 fails, so f is discontinuous at 2 (an infinite/essential discontinuity, since the function blows up). Naming WHICH condition fails is what earns the mark.

questions.question: Evaluate lim(x→∞) (3x² + x)/(5x² − 7) and state the general rule for rational functions at infinity.
questions.solution: Divide by x²: (3 + 1/x)/(5 − 7/x²) → 3/5. Rule: compare degrees — equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients; numerator degree higher → ±∞; denominator higher → 0. The dominant term is all that survives at infinity.

questions.question: Is every continuous function differentiable? Is every differentiable function continuous? Give the counterexample for the false one.
questions.solution: Differentiable ⇒ continuous (a derivative existing forces the function to be locally smooth). Continuous ⇏ differentiable: |x| is continuous everywhere but has no derivative at 0 — the left slope is −1, the right slope +1, so the difference quotient has no limit. Corner points are the standard counterexample.
